title: MongoDB Indexes: A Field Guide
summary: A dense, example-driven handbook on how MongoDB indexes actually work — B-tree mechanics, every index type from single field to TTL and text, and the prefix and sort-order rules that decide whether your query scans or seeks.

chapters.title: Why Indexes Exist
points: Without an index MongoDB does a COLLSCAN: reads every document in the collection to answer one query.
An index is an ordered data structure holding a small subset of fields plus a pointer to the full document (RecordId).
MongoDB indexes are B-trees (WiredTiger row-store B-trees), giving O(log n) lookup instead of O(n).
The `_id` index is created automatically on every collection, is unique, and cannot be dropped.
Indexes turn an equality lookup into a seek: descend the tree, land on the first matching key, walk siblings in order.
Because keys are stored sorted, one index serves equality, range (`$gt`, `$lt`, `$gte`, `$lte`), and sort — all three.
Trade-off: indexes cost disk, cost RAM in the WiredTiger cache, and slow every insert/update/delete that touches indexed fields.
Rule of thumb: each extra index adds write amplification; a 10-index collection does 11 B-tree writes per insert.
`db.coll.find({email:'a@b.com'}).explain('executionStats')` — read `totalDocsExamined` vs `nReturned`; a healthy index query has a ratio near 1:1.
Stage names to recognize: COLLSCAN (bad), IXSCAN (index seek), FETCH (load full doc), PROJECTION_COVERED (never touched the doc), SORT (in-memory blocking sort).
In-memory sorts are capped at 100 MB by default and abort with `Sort exceeded memory limit`; an index that provides the sort order removes the SORT stage entirely.
Indexes are per-collection, not per-database; a query can normally use only one index per predicate branch.
Create with `db.coll.createIndex({field: 1})`; 1 = ascending, -1 = descending.
Building an index on a live collection uses a hybrid build that yields to readers/writers, but still saturates I/O — schedule it.

chapters.title: Single Field Indexes
points: `db.users.createIndex({ age: 1 })` builds one B-tree keyed on `age`; every document contributes exactly one key.
Direction is irrelevant for a single field index: `{age: 1}` serves `sort({age: 1})` and `sort({age: -1})` equally, because the B-tree can be walked backwards.
Serves equality (`{age: 30}`), range (`{age: {$gte: 18, $lt: 65}}`), and `$in` (turned into a bounded multi-interval scan).
Index bounds appear in explain as `"age": ["[18, 65)"]` — tight bounds are good, `[MinKey, MaxKey]` means the index gave no selectivity.
Documents missing the field still get a key: `null` is indexed, so `{age: null}` matches both missing and explicitly-null fields.
Indexing a subdocument field uses dot notation: `createIndex({"address.city": 1})`.
Indexing a whole subdocument, `createIndex({address: 1})`, indexes the entire object — only matches whole-object equality, and field order inside the object matters.
Selectivity is what matters: an index on a boolean `isActive` field with 50/50 split rarely beats a collection scan.
Unique variant: `createIndex({email: 1}, {unique: true})` rejects duplicate keys with error code 11000 (`E11000 duplicate key error`).
Two documents both missing a uniquely-indexed field both index as `null` — the second insert fails. Use a partial index to allow many missing values.
Sparse variant: `{sparse: true}` skips documents lacking the field entirely, shrinking the index — but the index can no longer answer `{field: null}` or a full sort.
Partial index is the modern replacement for sparse: `createIndex({email:1},{unique:true, partialFilterExpression:{email:{$exists:true}}})`.
A partial index is only used when the query is provably a subset of `partialFilterExpression`.
Hidden indexes (`{hidden: true}`) stay maintained but invisible to the planner — test a drop safely, then unhide instantly if latency regresses.
Naming: auto-generated as `age_1`; pass `{name: 'idx_age'}` when the auto name would exceed the 127-byte limit.

chapters.title: Compound Indexes and the Prefix Rule
points: A compound index indexes multiple fields as one ordered key tuple: `createIndex({status: 1, createdAt: -1, userId: 1})`.
Keys sort lexicographically by the tuple — all `status` values grouped, and within each group ordered by `createdAt` descending.
Max 32 fields in a compound index.
Prefix rule: an index on `{a, b, c}` can serve queries on `{a}`, `{a,b}`, and `{a,b,c}` — the leading contiguous subset only.
It CANNOT efficiently serve `{b}` alone or `{b,c}` — no leading `a` means no way to seek; you'd need the whole tree.
A `{a,b,c}` index makes separate `{a}` and `{a,b}` indexes redundant — drop them.
ESR rule for field order: Equality first, then Sort fields, then Range fields.
Why ESR: equality pins a single contiguous slice; a range opens the slice, so anything after a range field is no longer in sorted order within the scan.
Example — `find({status:'active', age:{$gt:21}}).sort({createdAt:1})` wants `{status:1, createdAt:1, age:1}`, not `{status:1, age:1, createdAt:1}`.
The wrong order still uses the index for filtering but adds a blocking SORT stage — check explain for `stage: 'SORT'`.
Non-prefix fields can still be used as index filters after the seek (`IXSCAN` with loose bounds) — MongoDB may scan the index instead of the collection, cheaper but not a true seek.
Covered query: if every field the query reads and returns lives in the index, MongoDB never fetches the document. Requires `_id: 0` in the projection unless `_id` is in the index.
Covered queries show `totalDocsExamined: 0` — the strongest possible index win.
Index intersection exists (two indexes AND-ed) but is rarely chosen and usually loses to one well-ordered compound index.
Design compound indexes for query shapes, not for fields — list your top queries first, then build the minimum set of indexes that cover them.

chapters.title: Sort Order and Direction
points: Direction only matters in compound indexes, and only relative to the other fields.
`{a: 1, b: -1}` serves `sort({a: 1, b: -1})` (forward walk) and `sort({a: -1, b: 1})` (backward walk).
It does NOT serve `sort({a: 1, b: 1})` — that requires flipping one field independently, which a single tree walk cannot do.
Test: a sort is index-supported if the requested pattern equals the index pattern or its exact inverse (every field flipped).
A sort can only use an index if the sort keys form an index prefix, or follow equality-matched leading fields.
Equality absorbs a field: with `{status:1, createdAt:1}` and `find({status:'A'}).sort({createdAt:1})`, `status` is constant so `createdAt` behaves as the prefix.
A range predicate does NOT absorb a field — `find({status:{$gt:'A'}}).sort({createdAt:1})` still needs a blocking sort.
Blocking SORT means MongoDB buffers all results before returning the first — kills the latency of `limit(10)` queries.
With a supporting index, `sort().limit(10)` stops after 10 index entries — this is the classic pagination win.
`allowDiskUse: true` lets a big sort spill to disk instead of erroring, but it's a bandage, not a fix.
Sorting on a multikey (array) field via index is allowed but returns documents ordered by the array's min (asc) or max (desc) element.
`$natural` sort ignores indexes entirely and returns storage order — never rely on it for ordering semantics.
Collation affects sort order: an index built with a different collation than the query cannot serve that query's sort or equality.
Skip-heavy pagination (`skip(10000)`) still walks 10000 index entries; prefer range pagination on the sort key (`{createdAt: {$lt: lastSeen}}`).

chapters.title: Multikey Indexes (Arrays)
points: Index any field holding an array and MongoDB automatically makes it multikey — no special option, no separate command.
Multikey means one document produces N index keys, one per array element, all pointing back to the same RecordId.
`{tags: ['db','mongo','index']}` with `createIndex({tags:1})` inserts three keys: `db`, `mongo`, `index`.
Query `find({tags: 'mongo'})` seeks the single key — array membership becomes an ordinary equality lookup.
Index size grows with total array cardinality, not document count; a 1M-doc collection with 50-element arrays holds 50M keys.
Arrays of subdocuments: `createIndex({"items.sku": 1})` indexes each element's `sku`.
Hard limit: a compound index may contain AT MOST ONE array-valued field. Two arrays in one document would need a cartesian product of keys.
Inserting a document that makes two indexed fields arrays fails with `cannot index parallel arrays`.
The multikey flag is per-index and sticky: once set by any document, it stays set even after that document is deleted.
Multikey flag disables certain optimizations — notably index-only (covered) queries are impossible on a multikey index.
`$elemMatch` is required when multiple conditions must match the SAME array element: `find({items: {$elemMatch: {sku:'A', qty:{$gt:5}}}})`.
Without `$elemMatch`, `find({"items.sku":'A', "items.qty":{$gt:5}})` matches if DIFFERENT elements satisfy each condition — a classic silent bug.
The index can only narrow to one condition; the other is rechecked in the FETCH stage, so multikey bounds are often looser than they look.
Multikey indexes cannot be used for a sort when the sort field is the array field and the query also filters that array with a range.
TTL, hashed, and text indexes have their own array behavior; `unique` on a multikey field means no two DOCUMENTS may share any element value.

chapters.title: Text Indexes and Search
points: `createIndex({description: 'text'})` builds an inverted-style index over tokenized, stemmed, stop-word-filtered terms.
Only ONE text index per collection — but it may cover many fields: `createIndex({title:'text', body:'text'})`.
Wildcard form indexes every string field: `createIndex({"$**": 'text'})` — convenient, expensive, rarely right in production.
Query with `find({$text: {$search: 'mongodb index'}})` — the term list is OR-ed by default.
Phrase search uses escaped quotes: `$search: '\"compound index\"'`; negation uses a leading minus: `'mongodb -atlas'`.
Relevance score is available only via `{score: {$meta: 'textScore'}}` in the projection, and sortable with `sort({score:{$meta:'textScore'}})`.
Language drives stemming and stop words: `{default_language: 'english'}`, or per-document override via a `language` field.
`language: 'none'` disables stemming and stop-word removal — use for codes, identifiers, non-linguistic tokens.
Field weights control ranking: `{weights: {title: 10, body: 1}}` makes a title hit ten times more valuable.
A text index is implicitly multikey (each document yields many term keys) and is large — often bigger than the data it indexes.
Compound text indexes must put equality-only fields first: `{tenantId: 1, body: 'text'}`, and the query MUST supply `tenantId` as equality.
`$text` cannot be used inside `$or` with non-text clauses, cannot be negated with `$not`, and only one `$text` per query.
Text indexes do not support prefix/substring matching — searching `mongo` will not find `mongodb` unless stemming happens to collapse them.
For substring or fuzzy needs use Atlas Search (Lucene-backed) instead; `$text` is a blunt, self-hosted tool.
Case and diacritic insensitivity are on by default (version 3 text indexes); toggle with `caseSensitive` / `diacriticSensitive` query options.

chapters.title: TTL Indexes: Data That Expires
points: `createIndex({createdAt: 1}, {expireAfterSeconds: 3600})` deletes documents 3600s after their `createdAt` value.
The indexed field MUST be a BSON Date or an array of Dates; any other type means the document simply never expires.
With an array of Dates, the EARLIEST date in the array decides expiry.
A background thread (`TTLMonitor`) wakes every 60 seconds and deletes expired documents — so deletion latency is up to ~60s plus delete time.
TTL deletes are real deletes: they fire change streams, replicate via the oplog, and cost write I/O. A mass expiry is a write storm.
TTL only runs on the primary; secondaries expire documents by applying the replicated deletes, keeping replicas consistent.
Absolute-expiry pattern: set `expireAfterSeconds: 0` and store the exact desired deletion timestamp in the field.
Change the window without a rebuild: `db.runCommand({collMod:'sessions', index:{keyPattern:{createdAt:1}, expireAfterSeconds: 7200}})`.
A TTL index is a normal single-field index too — it still serves queries and sorts on that field.
Cannot be compound. Cannot be on `_id`. Cannot be applied to a capped collection.
Typical uses: sessions, verification tokens, rate-limit counters, event logs, caches, GDPR retention windows.
Deleted documents may still be returned by queries in the gap between expiry and the monitor's pass — filter defensively if exactness matters.
For high-volume time-series, a time-series collection with `expireAfterSeconds` drops whole buckets and is far cheaper than per-document TTL deletes.
Confirm the monitor is alive: `db.serverStatus().metrics.ttl` exposes `deletedDocuments` and `passes`.

chapters.title: The Rest of the Index Zoo
points: Hashed index: `createIndex({userId: 'hashed'})` stores a hash of the value — supports equality only, NO ranges and NO sorts.
Hashed indexes exist mainly to give an even shard key distribution for monotonically increasing values like ObjectId.
Wildcard index: `createIndex({"$**": 1})` indexes every field path; `createIndex({"user.$**": 1})` scopes it to a subtree.
Wildcard indexes suit unpredictable, user-defined schemas; they cannot be compound (pre-7.0), unique, TTL, or a shard key.
2dsphere index: `createIndex({loc: '2dsphere'})` over GeoJSON, for `$near`, `$geoWithin`, `$geoIntersects` on a spherical earth.
2d index: legacy flat coordinate pairs; use 2dsphere for anything new.
Unique index: enforces one document per key value; on a compound index the uniqueness applies to the whole key tuple, not each field.
Partial index: `{partialFilterExpression: {status: 'active'}}` indexes only matching documents — smaller index, lower write cost.
Partial + unique is the standard 'unique among active rows' pattern that SQL people expect from a filtered unique index.
Case-insensitive index: build with `{collation: {locale:'en', strength: 2}}`; queries must specify the same collation to use it.
Sparse vs partial: sparse only checks existence; partial takes an arbitrary predicate. Prefer partial.
Clustered collections (5.3+) store documents in `_id` order inside the index itself — no separate `_id` index, no FETCH for `_id` lookups.
Columnstore / Atlas Search indexes are separate products, not part of the core B-tree family.
Comparison row — Single: ranges+sort. Compound: multi-field+sort. Multikey: array membership. Text: token search. Hashed: equality+sharding. TTL: expiry. Wildcard: unknown schema. Geo: spatial.

chapters.title: Reading the Planner and Common Mistakes
points: `explain('executionStats')` is the only truth. `winningPlan` shows what ran; `rejectedPlans` shows what the planner considered.
Health check: `nReturned` ≈ `totalKeysExamined` ≈ `totalDocsExamined`. Big gaps mean wasted work.
The planner races candidate plans over a trial period, caches the winner per query shape, and re-evaluates after 10x work or on index change.
A cached bad plan explains 'it was fast yesterday' — inspect with `db.coll.getPlanCache().list()` and clear it if needed.
Mistake: leading wildcard regex. `/^abc/` uses the index; `/abc/` and `/.*abc/` cannot and force a scan.
Mistake: `$ne`, `$nin`, `$not` are non-selective — they must scan nearly the whole index because they match everything except a slice.
Mistake: type mismatch. `{userId: '123'}` never matches an indexed integer `123` — MongoDB does not coerce types.
Mistake: computed predicates. `{$expr: {$gt: ['$a', '$b']}}` and `$where` cannot use an index at all.
Mistake: `$or` needs an index on EVERY branch; one unindexed branch forces a collection scan for the whole query.
Mistake: unused and duplicate indexes. `$indexStats` shows access counts — `db.coll.aggregate([{$indexStats:{}}])` and drop the zeroes.
Mistake: index bloat from redundant prefixes — `{a:1}`, `{a:1,b:1}`, `{a:1,b:1,c:1}` should collapse to the longest.
Mistake: relying on `hint()` to fix a bad plan. Fix the index or the query; a hint hides the problem and breaks when data shifts.
Aggregation: only `$match` and `$sort` at the FRONT of the pipeline can use indexes; move them before `$group`/`$unwind`/`$project`.
`$lookup` uses an index on the FOREIGN collection's `foreignField` — build it or every join is a scan per input document.
Watch the working set: if `db.coll.totalIndexSize()` exceeds the WiredTiger cache, index pages thrash from disk and latency collapses.

chapters.title: Operating Indexes and the Cheat Sheet
points: Create in the background safely: since 4.2 all builds are hybrid — they take a brief exclusive lock at start and end, and yield in between.
On a replica set, an index build must complete on a majority of nodes before it commits; a failure on one node aborts everywhere.
`db.currentOp({'command.createIndexes':{$exists:true}})` shows build progress; `db.killOp(opid)` aborts it.
Rolling index build (take a secondary out of the set, build, rejoin, repeat) is the zero-impact method for huge production collections.
Inspect: `db.coll.getIndexes()` (definitions), `db.coll.stats().indexSizes` (bytes per index), `$indexStats` (usage counts).
Drop: `db.coll.dropIndex('idx_name')`. Hide it first (`collMod` with `hidden: true`), watch for a day, then drop.
Rebuild with `db.coll.reIndex()` only on standalone nodes and only to recover from corruption — it locks the collection.
Sizing rule: keep indexes plus the hot document working set inside the WiredTiger cache (default ~50% of RAM minus 1 GB).
Cheat sheet — index on `{a:1,b:1,c:1}` serves: `{a}`, `{a,b}`, `{a,b,c}`, `{a}+sort(b)`, `{a,b}+sort(c)`. Does not serve: `{b}`, `{c}`, `{b,c}`, `sort(b)` alone.
Cheat sheet — direction: single field ignores it; compound must match the sort pattern exactly or be its full inverse.
Cheat sheet — ESR: Equality, Sort, Range. Memorize it; it decides most compound field orders correctly.
Cheat sheet — arrays: automatic multikey, one array field per compound index, no covered queries, `$elemMatch` for per-element AND.
Cheat sheet — TTL: Date field only, `expireAfterSeconds`, ~60s granularity, single field, primary-driven deletes.
Cheat sheet — text: one per collection, OR-ed terms, `$meta: 'textScore'` for ranking, no substring matching.
Workflow: log slow queries (`db.setProfilingLevel(1, {slowms: 100})`), group by query shape, explain the worst, add ONE index, re-measure — never guess in batches.
